newsitem.title: USA: US flow-control backers face uphill battle on Hill.
newsitem.headline: US flow-control backers face uphill battle on Hill.

text.p: Backers of federal flow-control legislation have an uphill battle this year in getting a measure cleared by the U.S. Congress, the chairman of a key U.S. Senate subcommittee said on Tuesday.

"Frankly, the supporters of flow control have a much tougher case to prove this year," Sen Bob Smith, a Republican from New Hampshire, said at a Senate Environment and Public Works Committee hearing on interstate waste and flow control.
Smith chairs the committee's subpanel on Superfund, waste control and risk assessment.

Flow control refers to the ability of local governments to direct solid waste to specific facilities that are financed by tax-exempt bonds. The U.S. Supreme Court in 1994 said that flow control violates the U.S. Constitution because it impedes interstate trade.

Smith said that during the last Congress, he backed grandfathering a limited number of flow-control facilities because he was "influenced" by the testimony of a number of local governments who warned that their tax-exempt waste facility bonds would default without a bill.

"Despite our good intentions, lobbyists who supported flow control were not satisfied with our common-sense provisions, and worked hard to organize a number of harmful amendments" that contributed to the bill's "ultimate demise," Smith said.
"It is because of this experience that I am wary of efforts to provide any grandfathering authority whatsoever," he said.

Smith signalled that Congress will not fall for a "sky-is-falling" approach this year from flow-control backers. "During the last Congress, we had witnesses who testified that we had to act 'immediately' to protect municipalities from having to default on bonds they had issued to fund their waste-to-energy facilities, landfill construction and recycling efforts," Smith said.

"Now we are here two years later, and, surprise, surprise, the sky has not fallen," Smith said. "While only 18 (credit) downgrades have taken place nationwide -- almost all in 1995 -- widespread municipal defaults did not occur. These bonds have remained stable because municipalities have ... instituted competitive tipping fees, cut their overhead costs, and sought alternative streams of revenue. That is the way the free market should work."
